questions.title: Facultative parasite can live outside or inside a host
questions.question: Type of parasite that can live outside the host and can also be parasitic?

explanations.A: Incorrect. An obligate parasite cannot live outside a host at all -- the opposite of the flexibility this stem describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An incidental parasite is a genuine infection of an unusual host species, not one defined by living either freely or parasitically.
explanations.C: Correct. A facultative parasite can live either freely in the environment or parasitically inside a host. It switches between the two lifestyles depending on conditions, rather than being locked into one. This flexibility distinguishes it from an obligate parasite, which has no free-living option at all.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A pseudoparasite is not a real parasite at all, merely an artefact mistaken for one.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a facultative parasite as one that can live either freely or parasitically.
questions.source_citation: INI MCQ .pdf, Introduction to parasitology, p84

questions.title: Obligate parasite cannot live outside a host
questions.question: Type of parasite that can't live outside the host's body?

explanations.A: Correct. An obligate parasite is completely dependent on its host. It cannot survive outside a host at any stage of its life cycle. This total dependency is what distinguishes it from a facultative parasite, which retains a free-living option.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Temporary" describes the duration/pattern of host contact (e.g. a temporary ectoparasite that feeds and leaves), not an inability to survive outside a host altogether.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A facultative parasite CAN live outside a host -- the opposite of what this stem describes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A pseudoparasite is not a real parasite and is not defined by host dependency at all.

questions.learning_objective: Identify an obligate parasite as one that cannot live outside the host's body.
questions.source_citation: INI MCQ .pdf, Introduction to parasitology, p84

questions.title: Vector may act as intermediate, definitive or transfer host
questions.question: May act as intermediate host, or definitive host or transfer host?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Incidental host" names a single specific role (an unusual host species), not an organism that can play several different life-cycle roles.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A paratenic host is itself one specific role (arrested development, onward carriage), not the umbrella category being described.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Transfer host" is likewise one specific role, a synonym of paratenic host, not the broader category.
explanations.D: Correct. A vector, typically an arthropod, actively shares in a parasite's life cycle. Depending on the organism, it can act biologically as an intermediate host that supports development, or even as a definitive host, as the mosquito is for the sexual stage of Plasmodium. It can also act as a purely mechanical transfer host, simply carrying the organism without any development at all.

questions.learning_objective: State that a vector can act as an intermediate, definitive or transfer host depending on the parasite.
questions.source_citation: INI MCQ .pdf, Introduction to parasitology, p84

questions.title: Vector defined as an arthropod active in the life cycle
questions.question: Name that is given to arthropods that share actively in the life cycle of the parasite?

explanations.A: Correct. A vector is the name given to an arthropod that shares actively in a parasite's life cycle. It transmits the parasite between hosts, moving it forward through the cycle. For a biological vector, it also supports part of the parasite's own development, unlike a purely mechanical carrier.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Incidental" describes an unusual host species for a given parasite, not an arthropod transmitter.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Transfer" (paratenic) describes a host of arrested development, not specifically an actively participating arthropod.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A reservoir host is a non-human animal source of human infection, not necessarily an arthropod or a transmitter.

questions.learning_objective: State that a vector is the name for an arthropod that shares actively in a parasite's life cycle.

questions.title: Opportunistic parasite causes disease in immunocompromised hosts
questions.question: Opportunistic parasite?

options.A: Lives in another habitat than normal
options.C: Passes through the alimentary canal without being noticed
options.D: Lives in another host than normal

explanations.A: Incorrect. Living in another habitat than normal describes an erratic (aberrant) parasite, not an opportunistic one.
explanations.B: Correct. An opportunistic parasite is normally kept in check by an intact immune system. It causes disease specifically in immunocompromised hosts, when that check is lost. Cryptosporidium and Strongyloides are classic examples, both capable of severe, even life-threatening disease once immunity is impaired.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Passing through the alimentary canal unnoticed describes a coprozoic organism, not an opportunistic parasite.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Living in another host than normal describes an incidental (accidental) parasite, a different category from opportunism, which is about the host's immune status rather than which species is infected.

questions.learning_objective: Identify an opportunistic parasite as one causing disease specifically in immunocompromised hosts.
questions.source_citation: INI MCQ .pdf, Introduction to parasitology, p85

questions.title: Parasitism: one benefits, the other is harmed
questions.question: Parasitism means relationship between two animals in which?

options.C: One partner benefits and the other is harmed
options.D: One partner benefits and the other not

explanations.A: Incorrect. Two partners both being harmed does not describe any of the standard host-microbe relationship categories taught here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Both partners benefiting describes mutualism, not parasitism.
explanations.C: Correct. In parasitism, one partner, the parasite, benefits at the expense of the other, the host. The host is harmed by the relationship, not merely unaffected. This exploitative pattern is what distinguishes parasitism from commensalism, where the host is unaffected, and mutualism, where both benefit.
explanations.D: Incorrect. One partner benefiting while the other is simply unaffected (neither helped nor harmed) describes commensalism, not parasitism.

questions.learning_objective: Define parasitism as a relationship in which one partner benefits and the other is harmed.
questions.source_citation: INI MCQ .pdf, Introduction to parasitology, p85

questions.title: Commensalism: one benefits, the other is unaffected
questions.question: Commensalism is a relationship between two partners in which?

options.C: One partner benefits and the other is harmed
options.D: One partner benefits and the other not

explanations.A: Incorrect. Two partners both being harmed does not describe any of the standard host-microbe relationship categories taught here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Both partners benefiting describes mutualism, not commensalism.
explanations.C: Incorrect. One partner benefiting while the other is harmed describes parasitism, not commensalism.
explanations.D: Correct. In commensalism, one partner benefits while the other is neither helped nor harmed. "Benefits and the other not" (affected) is the standard shorthand for this pattern. It sits between parasitism, where the host is harmed, and mutualism, where both partners benefit.

questions.learning_objective: Define commensalism as a relationship in which one partner benefits and the other is unaffected.
